To form the perfect subjunctive: haya / hayas / haya… + participle.
To react to things that have already happened: me alegra que hayas venido, no creo que lo haya hecho.
To form the pluperfect subjunctive: hubiera / hubieras… + participle.
To express regrets and hypotheses about the past: si hubiera sabido, habría venido; ojalá hubiera…
To review all four tenses of the subjunctive.
June, Bucharest. Ana and Mihai have news. They make a video call with both mothers at once: Carmen in Madrid and Elena in Brașov. Mihai translates.
Hello, darlings! What’s happened? I was surprised you called on a Tuesday morning.
Mum, Elena… we have something to tell you. Mihai, you translate, I can’t.
All right. Mum, Carmen: Ana is pregnant. You’re going to be grandmothers.
What?! I can’t believe it! Oh my God! Pepe, come here, we’re going to be grandparents!
Mum says it’s the happiest day of her life. And that she’s glad we waited until the second trimester to tell. It’s a Romanian tradition.
The second trimester? How long have you known?
For three months, Mum. I’m sorry. We wanted to be sure.
Three months! If you’d told me earlier, I’d have knitted three jumpers by now. If only you’d told me at Christmas!
At Christmas we didn’t know yet, Mum.
All right, all right… And is it a boy or a girl?
A girl. The gynaecologist told us last week, at the scan.
Mum is asking if we’ve already chosen the name. She hopes we haven’t picked a “too modern” name.
We thought of Rosa Elena. Rosa after Grandma Rosario, and Elena after you, Elena.
Rosa Elena… Beautiful. Grandma’s going to faint when she finds out. I’m so glad you thought of her.
And Mum says she doesn’t think there’s ever been a baby with two more meddling grandmothers.
Tell her she’s right! And to get ready!

“se alegra de que” = is glad that
“si me lo hubieras dicho” = if you’d told me (pluperfect subj.)
“le va a dar algo” = she’s going to faint (with emotion)
The h is silent: A-ya, oo-BYEH-ra. Don’t confuse them with “allá” (over there), which sounds like “haya” in many regions!
“¡No me lo puedo creer!” Your voice rises sharply on “puedo” and falls on “creer”. Spaniards exaggerate their intonation when they’re happy.
em-ba-ra-THA-da. ⚠️ “Embarazada” does NOT mean “embarrassed” (that’s “avergonzada”)! It’s one of the most famous traps for English speakers.
It’s the subjunctive partner of “he hecho” (pretérito perfecto, chapter 13). It’s formed with the subjunctive of HABER + participle:
You use it when you react (emotion, doubt, wish) to something that HAS ALREADY HAPPENED, and the main verb is in the present:
I’m glad you’ve come. (you’re already here)
I don’t think he did it.
I hope you’ve had a rest.
2. Present or perfect? When the action happens
Me alegra que vengas. (you’re coming now / you’ll come)
Me alegra que hayas venido. (you’ve already come)
Espero que apruebes. (the exam is in the future)
Espero que hayas aprobado. (the exam has happened)
No creo que lo haya sabido.
A simple question: does the action come before the moment I’m speaking? If so, haya + participle.
It’s formed with the imperfect subjunctive of HABER (hubiera) + participle. You use it for the unreal past: what WOULD HAVE happened.
Hypotheses about the past: si + HUBIERA + participle, HABRÍA + participle. Exactly like English “if I HAD known, I WOULD HAVE…”.
If you’d told me, I’d have helped you.
In speech, many Spaniards use hubiera in both halves: Si lo hubiera sabido, hubiera venido. It’s accepted.
4. Regrets: ojalá hubiera, me habría gustado que
If only you’d told me! (but you didn’t)
I’d have liked my grandfather to meet her.
It bothered me that they hadn’t told me.
Don’t confuse “ojalá hayas…” (I hope you’ve… — possible, I don’t know yet) with “ojalá hubieras…” (I wish you had… — I know it didn’t happen).

recent past, main verb in the present

Un mensaje de la abuela Rosario
An hour after the call, Ana gets a voice message from Grandma Rosario. Here it is, transcribed.
Anita, darling: your mother has just told me. I had to sit down, because my legs went weak.
Rosa? Are you really going to give her my name? I can’t believe you thought of an old woman like me.
If only your grandfather Andrés had lived to see this. If he were here, he’d already have baked bread for the whole neighbourhood.
I’m so glad you’ve found a man who loves you the way he loved me.
One thing, darling: when the little one is born, I want you to sing her the song from the fiesta. The one I danced to with your grandfather. That way she’ll know where she comes from.
And tell Mihai that if she turns out as stubborn as you, he’d better be ready. I love you, my darling.

¿Qué canción quiere la abuela que Ana le cante a la niña?
In July, Ana and Mihai went back to Grandpa Gheorghe’s village. Ana was already five months pregnant, and the narrow road seemed longer than ever.
This time Grandpa wasn’t waiting at the gate. Mihai got worried. It was the first time in thirty years that his grandfather hadn’t come out to meet him.
Lup, the huge dog, was there. He ran up to Ana, sniffed her belly very carefully and then sat down next to her, very seriously, as if he were her bodyguard.
They found Grandpa in the barn behind the house. He was sitting on a little stool, surrounded by wood shavings, with a small knife in his hand.
In front of him was a cradle. A cradle of pale wood, still unfinished, with flowers and stars carved on the sides.
“Bunicule…” said Mihai, and couldn’t say anything else.
Grandpa looked up and smiled. He said something in Romanian, and Mihai translated in a broken voice:
“He says to forgive him for not coming out to meet us. He wanted the cradle to be ready before we arrived, but his hands aren’t as quick as they used to be.”
Ana went closer and touched the wood. It was smooth and warm, as if it were alive. At the head, Grandpa had carved a she-bear. A big she-bear, with a little cub asleep between her paws.
Grandpa nodded. He spoke again, slowly. Mihai translated sentence by sentence.
“This cradle is made from a walnut tree my father planted the year I was born. If I’d cut it down earlier, I’d have made furniture to sell. But I didn’t cut it down. I didn’t know why. Now I know.”
“My children slept in this wood. Well, in a cradle made from its branches. Then Mihai’s father used it too. It broke many years ago. I regretted not keeping it.”

“So when I found out you were having a little girl, I thought: this time I’ll make it from the trunk. So it lasts a hundred years. So my great-grandchildren can sleep in it, and my great-grandchildren’s children.”
Ana’s cheeks were wet with tears. She knelt down slowly beside Grandpa and took his hands. They were rough, covered in little cuts.
“Mulțumesc,” she said, in her best Romanian. “Mulțumesc, bunicule.” (Thank you, Grandpa.)

They spent the whole week in the village. Every morning, Grandpa worked on the cradle. Mihai helped him sand the wood. Ana, sitting in the shade with Lup at her feet, read them a book of Spanish stories out loud.
Grandpa didn’t understand a word, but he asked her to keep reading. He said the little girl needed to hear Spanish in the womb, so she wouldn’t feel a stranger in either of her two countries.
On the last day, the cradle was ready. Grandpa gave it a coat of clear varnish that smelled of the forest. Then, with a nail, he wrote something underneath, where nobody could see it.
“What did he write?” Ana asked Mihai.
Mihai bent down to read it. He took a moment before answering.
“He’s written: ‘Pentru Rosa Elena’ (For Rosa Elena). ‘So that you’re never cold.’”
The cradle travelled to Bucharest on the car roof, wrapped in blankets, tied with three ropes. Mihai drove so slowly that even the tractors overtook them.
In the flat, they put it by the window, under the wall with Andrei’s drawings. Ana stood looking at it for a long time.
“You know what?” she said to Mihai. “If someone had told me four years ago, when I joined that Japanese club, that I’d end up here…”
“No. But I’m so glad it happened.”
That night, for the first time, Ana felt the baby move. It was a tiny movement, like the flutter of a butterfly’s wings. Or like a bear cub waking up in a walnut cradle.
Ana woke Mihai with a little cry. He put his hand on her belly and waited. For a minute nothing happened. Then, again: a little kick, light, almost shy.
“Hello, Rosa Elena,” Mihai whispered, in Spanish and then in Romanian. “Bienvenida. Bine ai venit.”
The next day they called Grandpa to tell him. He listened in silence and then said just one sentence, which Mihai didn’t need to translate, because Ana already understood it: “Știam eu.” (I knew it.)

Ana, Mihai: we’ve just heard. We can’t believe you’re going to be parents! Well, actually we can. Yuki says she knew from the club’s first day.

A letter to a child of the future

Write a 15-sentence letter to a child (yours, a grandchild or an imaginary child) who will read it in 18 years’ time. Tell them what you’re glad has happened (perfect subj.), what you regret (si hubiera… / ojalá hubiera…), what you hope for them and what you’d do if you were their age again. Use ALL 4 subjunctive tenses.
